prompt: we sell meal kits by subscription, 70 a box. after food, packing and delivery about 40% of the box price is left, so around 28. a competitor dropped their price 18% this week and my cofounder wants to match it tomorrow. talk me through whether we should.
rubric: Works out what matching does to the box: new price about 57.40, leaving about 15.40 a box instead of 28 (costs stay at 42).
States the break-even: roughly 82% more boxes (28 / 15.40) just to earn the same total, and says that is very unlikely to come from matching.
Takes a position (do not simply match everyone tomorrow) rather than listing pros and cons and leaving it open.
Asks or says what to check first: whether customers are actually leaving or only the competitor's ad is loud, and how similar the two products are.
Offers a narrower alternative to an across-the-board cut, such as a targeted offer for at-risk customers, a smaller or cheaper box, or holding the price and saying why it is worth it.

prompt: marketing wants 25% off our yearly plan (240 a year) for all of next month to hit the quarter target. roughly 80% of the plan price is margin. is it worth it?
rubric: Computes the per-sale effect: 240 becomes 180, and margin falls from about 192 to about 132 per plan.
States the break-even: about 45% more yearly sales (192 / 132) just to earn the same margin as without the discount.
Points out that people who would have bought at full price anyway also get the discount, and that a month-long discount to everyone also pulls forward sales or trains people to wait.
Gives a clear answer (not as proposed, or only under stated conditions) rather than leaving the decision open.
Suggests a narrower or cheaper way to hit the target, such as limiting to new customers, a shorter window, or adding value instead of cutting price.

prompt: our hosting bill went up about a third this year. hosting is around a fifth of what we charge per seat (30 a seat). how much should we raise our price, and what reason can we honestly give?
rubric: Works out the cost increase per seat: hosting about 6 goes to about 8, so about 2 more a seat, which is about 7% of the 30 price, not a third.
Says plainly that a price rise of about a third is not justified by this cost alone, and that roughly 2 a seat (or a rounded figure near it) restores the margin in money terms.
Gives a reason that is true and in proportion: hosting costs rose and the change is sized to cover that; does not blame hosting for a larger rise than it explains.
Notes that if they want to raise by more, they should give the other real reason (more features, support, value) instead of attributing it to hosting.
Mentions practical handling such as advance notice to existing customers.

prompt: finance says every seat in our evening workshops costs us 210 once rent, staff and marketing are spread across the seats (4200 a session, 20 seats), so they won't allow a 150 student price. most weeks the room is half empty. materials are about 15 a head on top. who is right?
rubric: Explains that 210 is an average that spreads costs that do not change when one more person sits down: the 4200 is the same whether 10 or 20 come.
Computes what an extra student at 150 actually adds: about 135 after the 15 of materials, which is more than nothing while seats are empty.

Does not simply side with the student price: raises the risk that people who would pay full price switch to it, and suggests a limit (proof of student status, off-peak sessions, or only seats unsold close to the date).
Says finance is right about one thing: over time the average price across all seats still has to cover the 4200, so a half-empty room at current prices loses money and needs its own fix.
Gives a clear verdict (for example: allow the price with limits, and judge it by added money per session, not by the 210).

prompt: write a two-line banner for our spring candle sale: 15% off everything until the end of april.
rubric: Delivers exactly a two-line banner (or a very small number of two-line options), ready to paste.
States the 15% off and the end-of-april deadline correctly.
Adds no facts that were not given, such as a discount code, free shipping, a limited stock claim or a named product.
Does not lecture about margins, break-even or whether the sale is a good idea, and does not ask a list of questions before writing.
Wording is plain and does not use fake urgency beyond the stated end date.

prompt: we sell a downloadable font family for 40 and almost all of that is profit. we want to drop it to 30 for launch week to get noticed. any reason not to?
rubric: Says go ahead (or go ahead with minor care) without a long list of warnings; the cut is small, short and nearly free to the seller.
Notes the break-even is modest: at 30 instead of 40 about a third more sales (40 / 30) covers it, and the launch attention is plausibly worth that.
Recommends making the end date clear and sticking to it, and being honest that 30 is a launch price.
Keeps the answer short and proportionate; does not demand surveys, elasticity modelling or a test design for a one-week promotion.
May mention one cheap thing to watch (for example, people who bought at 40 just before) without making it a blocker.

prompt: we run a coffee subscription, 600 subscribers at 18 a bag. each bag costs us about 11 all in (beans, roasting, bag, shipping) and green coffee just got more expensive. thinking of going to 20 but i'm scared half of them will cancel. should i do it?
rubric: Computes the margin: 7 a bag now, 9 at 20, so monthly margin goes from 4200 to 5400 if nobody leaves.
States the break-even: they can lose about 22% of subscribers (about 133 of 600) before total margin falls below 4200 (4200 / 9 is about 467 subscribers).
Puts the fear in proportion: losing half would hurt, but the more likely loss is far below the break-even, and says what would make it likely to be larger or smaller.
Gives a clear recommendation (raise, or raise by a smaller step such as 19) rather than leaving it open.
Suggests honest handling: advance notice, a plain true reason (bean costs), and watching cancellations in the first month or testing on new subscribers first.

prompt: critique my plan. i run a bike shop. a big online store sells the same helmet 12% cheaper than us. helmet is 100 here and costs us 70. my manager wants a price-match guarantee on everything we sell, printed on the door, so nobody walks out to buy online. i think it's fine because it only applies if they ask.
rubric: Works out the helmet case: matching means 88, margin falls from 30 to 18 per helmet, so the shop needs about 67% more helmet sales to earn the same, if every sale were matched.

Distinguishes a match on request (costs only the sales where someone asks) from lowering the shelf price (costs every sale), and says the plan is closer to the first but a sign on the door invites many more asks.
Names limits that make a guarantee affordable: same model, in stock, from named local or authorised sellers, with proof, not on clearance, and perhaps not on everything.
Considers what the match is worth beyond the helmet (a customer who stays to buy lights, locks, servicing) and what it risks (being undercut permanently by a rival's price).
Gives a clear verdict on the plan rather than a balanced list.

prompt: need a short note for the shop page. our sticker packs go from 4.00 to 4.25 on 1 june because paper and postage both cost more now. keep it friendly and honest, nothing fancy.
rubric: States the old price (4.00), the new price (4.25) and the date (1 june) correctly.
Gives the reason as paper and postage costs, plainly and without exaggerating or adding other reasons.
Is short (a few sentences) and friendly, with no grovelling apology and no fake urgency.
Adds no facts that were not given, such as a sale at the old price, a discount code, a percentage claim or a promise about future prices.
Does not argue with the decision, ask for demand data or add a break-even analysis; the request is for the note.
